Residents cannot opt out of government. They cannot take their benefits, permits or tax affairs to a competitor, so their trust is not a market signal - it is a democratic one. Lose it and the costs are concrete: forms returned half-empty, advice ignored, consultations boycotted, staff abused, and every honest service redesign read as a trick.
Competence: decisions are right, letters are accurate, systems work. AI raises competence only where accuracy is measured (Volumes 2-8); unmeasured AI lowers it at scale.
Honesty: the service says what AI does, where it errs and what it will never do - before being asked, in the register (p14).
Benevolence: residents believe the service is on their side. That belief is built by frontline staff who have time, discretion and support - a workforce question before it is a communications one.
Answerability: a named person can explain, apologise and put things right (p17, 20). Anonymous systems cannot be trusted because they cannot answer.
Trust is a stock, not a flow: built slowly by kept promises, spent quickly by hidden ones.
Trust in AI follows trust in the institution, not the reverse. Fix the institution's promises first.
Never announce trust. Publish the evidence - accuracy, overturns, complaints - and let trust be the conclusion residents draw.
Low trust is information about the service, not a defect in the public. Treat survey anger as casework about the institution.

20 Golden Rules for workforce, ethics and public trust
1. AI prepares, drafts and flags; people serve, decide and answer.
2. Trust is a stock: built by kept promises, spent by hidden ones.
3. No decision about a person's livelihood, selection or standing is automated - inside the house or outside it.
4. Subtraction before addition: work leaves the day before tools join it.
5. The time AI saves is allocated in advance, in writing, with staff representatives.
6. Nobody signs what they cannot challenge; training precedes access, assessment precedes sign-off.
7. The override is one action, needs no permission, and its reasons are read as evidence about the tool first.
8. Very high agreement with AI is a warning to investigate, not a success to celebrate.
9. Ethics review can say no, sometimes does, and publishes that it did.
10. A fairness disparity is a defect: owned, fixed, re-tested - or publicly reasoned.
11. Say it before you are asked: uses, limits, errors and failures, on your own timetable.
12. Never say the computer decided. Name the person, the evidence and the route to challenge.
13. The human route is always open, without penalty, and its use is published.
14. Remedy before explanation; apologise specifically; thank the complainant who was right.
15. Never target fewer complaints. Target fewer causes.
16. No surveillance scoring of staff or residents - excluded, not minimised.
17. Leaders use the tools they mandate, front the failures personally, and never shield behind frontline staff.
18. Publish trust, fairness and workforce results with the savings, in the same document.
19. When trust fails: pause, tell affected people directly, repair proactively, publish the cause.
20. Write every record for the future reader - the auditor, the panel, the resident, the inquiry.

strategy
Government does not get to move fast and break things

A private firm that ships a bad model loses customers. A government that ships a bad model denies a benefit, misfiles a permit, or flags an innocent taxpayer - and the resident cannot take their business elsewhere. That asymmetry is the whole strategy. AI in government is adopted at the speed of trust, and trust is built with evidence, published in plain language, one service at a time.
Read pages 4-7 first. They carry the thesis, the value test and the stop list. If a proposal fails there, nothing later in the book rescues it.
Work the gates in order. S0 Mandate, S1 Portfolio, S2 Design, S3 Readiness, S4 Proof, S5 Scale. A gate is a decision with named evidence, not a stage a project drifts through.
Fill the templates as you go. Templates 1-8 on pages 30-31 are the working record. A strategy that exists only in slides will not survive an audit, an election, or a change of administration.
Keep the lenses honest. Executive, Service and Accountability callouts appear throughout. When the three lenses disagree, that disagreement is the decision - surface it, do not average it away.
The one-sentence strategy: automate the queue, the document and the lookup first; assist the
caseworker second; and never automate the judgement a resident has a legal right to appeal.
Fund trust before capability. The first budget line is evaluation and transparency, not licences.
Start where residents already wait: phones unanswered, forms returned, permits stalled.
Every claim in this book must be producible later - to an auditor, a court, or a public records request.

Promise. Within three years, Northbridge residents get an answer on first contact for the ten highest- volume services, caseworkers spend their time on judgement instead of transcription, and every automated step in a public decision can be explained, logged and appealed.
1. Service outcomes, not model counts. The portfolio is judged on wait time, error rate, completion rate
and fairness gaps - never on how many AI tools were deployed.
2. Assist before automate, automate before decide. Copilots for staff first, automation of mechanical
3. One front door, every channel. Web, phone, in person and paper all reach the same case record.
Digital-only is a policy choice to exclude, and this strategy does not make it.
4. Public by default. A public register of AI systems, what they do, what data they use and how to
appeal. Secrecy is reserved for genuine security and fraud-detection detail.
5. Bought, not captured. Open standards, exportable data, exit clauses and evaluation rights in every
contract, so the state can change supplier without rebuilding the service.
Northbridge baseline (illustrative): 1.1 million contacts a year, 38 percent about a case already open;
average permit review 74 days; benefits error rate 6.1 percent, mostly missing documents, not fraud. The
Say the promise in resident outcomes and put a date on it. Vague ambition cannot be audited.
Publish the baseline before you start. A baseline published afterwards is marketing.
If a resident cannot tell what changed, the programme has not delivered, whatever the dashboard says.
strategy

AI pays in government where the work is voluminous, repetitive and verifiable - where a correct answer exists, the evidence is in the file, and a human can check a sample and know whether the system is right.
Contact centres Retrieval over published guidance, call summarisation, translation
First-contact resolution rises; advice stays sourced to published text
Benefits intake Document checks, missing-evidence prompts, form pre-fill
Most errors are missing documents; catching them at intake cuts rework and hardship
Permitting Completeness checks, code lookup, review summaries
Reviewers start from a checked file instead of an incomplete one
Tax and revenue Case prioritisation, correspondence drafting, anomaly triage
Officers work the highest-risk cases first; residents get clearer letters
Records and FOI Search, redaction assistance, disclosure logs
Statutory deadlines met without burning out the records team
Dispatchers keep judgement; the record writes itself
Internal operations Meeting records, procurement drafting, HR policy lookup
Frees professional time across every department at low risk
The pattern is consistent: AI removes waiting, searching and re-typing. It does not remove the accountable officer, and in the paying use cases it does not need to.
Rank opportunities by resident pain multiplied by volume, not by vendor enthusiasm.
Intake and triage are the safest high-value ground in the whole portfolio.
Every paying use case produces its own evaluation data. If it cannot be checked, it does not pay - it merely runs.
strategy
Where AI does not pay, and classical controls govern

Some government work must stay human, rule-based, or both - because the law requires a decision- maker, because the data encodes past injustice, or because the cost of a confident wrong answer falls on someone with no recourse.
Benefit eligibility decisions Statutory discretion and appeal rights attach to a named decision-maker
Past enforcement patterns encode where the state looked, not where harm is
Published risk criteria, human selection, disparate-impact testing
Consequences are irreversible and evidence is contested
Decision support only, with the social worker's judgement recorded as final
Political and policy choices Democratic accountability cannot be delegated to a model
Liberty interests; opaque scores cannot be cross-examined
Final fraud determinations An accusation by algorithm denies due process in practice
AI triages; investigators establish facts; notices state evidence and appeal route
Rule of thumb: if a resident would be entitled to ask "who decided this, and on what
evidence?" - a person must be able to answer, with the record in hand.
A use case on the stop list is not a pilot opportunity. It is a closed door.
Hold the stop list publicly. It is the cheapest trust the programme will ever buy.
Review the list annually, in public, and record what was added or removed and why.
strategy
The public value test: five questions, all must pass
Every proposed use case answers five questions in writing before it enters the portfolio. One failure stops it until the failure is fixed or the proposal is withdrawn.
1. Problem. What resident or staff problem, measured today, does this solve? A baseline number is
required - a wait, an error rate, a backlog, a cost per case.
2. Legality. What statute, regulation or policy authorises this use of data and this kind of decision
support? Name it. "Innovation" is not a legal basis.
3. Fairness. Who could be made worse off, and how will you know? Name the groups, the test and the
4. Reversibility. If the system is wrong at scale, how are affected residents found, notified and made
whole? If there is no answer, there is no deployment.
5. Value. What does the whole thing cost over five years - licences, data work, evaluation, staff time, exit
- against what measured benefit? Optimism is not a benefit.
Northbridge example: benefits intake assistance passed all five - a measured 6.1 percent error rate,
clear statutory basis for intake processing, fairness testing by language and disability status, full
reversibility because officers still decide, and a five-year cost below the rework it removes. Automated
eligibility scoring failed questions 2, 3 and 4 and was withdrawn at the test, before any vendor was
Apply the test before procurement. Afterwards, sunk cost argues louder than evidence.
Make the answers public for anything resident-facing. Sunlight is a control.
A withdrawn proposal is the test working, not failing. Count withdrawals as a success metric.
strategy
S0 Mandate: a named political sponsor, a named accountable officer, a legal basis and a funded evaluation line - or the work does not start.
A sponsor at cabinet or executive-board level who will defend the programme in public, including when a pilot is stopped.
An accountable service owner, by name, whose performance objectives include the resident outcome - not the delivery date alone.
A written legal review covering data use, decision rights, records retention and appeal routes.
Funding that explicitly includes evaluation, accessibility, translation and the cost of the non-digital channels that must keep running.
A communications commitment: the AI register entry is drafted before the build starts.
The sponsor is a vendor, a consultancy, or "the innovation team" with no service owner attached.
The business case counts staff savings from posts that no one has agreed to change.
The timeline is set by an announcement date rather than by evidence milestones.
Your name is on this. If you would not defend it on the record, do not mandate it.
A mandate that names an owner protects frontline staff when something goes wrong.
Auditors start at the mandate. A clean S0 record makes every later review shorter.
strategy

Every candidate use case is scored on the same six factors, in the open, by a panel that includes the service owner, a data specialist, a frontline representative and an accountability reviewer. Scores and reasons are recorded in Template 2.
Resident pain 25% Long waits, high failure demand, hardship caused by delay or error
15% Thousands of similar cases with a stable, published rule set
Evidence readiness 20% Clean case data, a checkable correct answer, an existing quality sample
Risk and reversibility 20% Errors are detectable, correctable and compensable; no liberty or livelihood decision
Equity effect 10% Narrows an access gap - language, disability, digital exclusion - rather than widening it
Deliverability 10% One accountable owner, one system of record, no unresolved inter-agency dispute

Risk is scored inversely: the higher the harm if wrong, the lower the score, and any use case on the stop list (page 6) is excluded before scoring begins. A charismatic pitch cannot outscore a weak evidence base, because evidence readiness and risk together carry 40 percent of the weight.
Inside a Northbridge service centre: assisted digital help beside staffed counters, one case record across every channel.
Publish the scores. A portfolio that cannot be explained will not be defended.
Score with the frontline in the room; they know where the failure demand hides.
Re-score annually. Yesterday's safe pilot is not automatically tomorrow's safe scale-up.
strategy

Internal and intake use cases with a human deciding everything: contact-centre retrieval and summarisation, benefits document checks, records search and redaction assistance, staff policy copilots. Goal: evaluation machinery that works, a public register that is real, and two or three services with published before-and-after numbers.

Resident-facing assistance with guardrails: guided applications, multilingual service guidance, permit completeness checks, appointment and queue optimisation. Goal: measurable equity gains - completion rates rising fastest for the groups previously worst served.

Cross-service work: tell-us-once data sharing with consent and a record, proactive entitlement prompts (a human confirms before any payment changes), joined-up case views for complex cases. Goal: residents stop being the integration layer between agencies.
Sequencing rule: a wave starts when the previous wave's published results justify it, not when the
calendar says so. Skipping Wave 1's evaluation discipline to reach Wave 3's ambition is how programmes
Waves are evidence commitments. Tie funding release to published results.
Wave 1 looks unglamorous and is where the programme is actually won.
Each wave's exit criteria belong in the public register, not an internal deck.
strategy
S1 Portfolio: every funded use case has passed the public value test, scored in the open, and fits inside the delivery and evaluation capacity that actually exists.
Public value test answers (Template 1) filed for every use case, including the ones rejected, with reasons.
Scoring sheets (Template 2) signed by the full panel, dissent recorded rather than smoothed over.
A capacity check: named evaluation, data and service-design staff matched to the portfolio size. Ten pilots with one evaluator is a plan to learn nothing ten times.
A balance check: at least half the portfolio in Wave 1 risk territory for the first year.
A kill list from last cycle: what was stopped, what it cost, what was learned - presented alongside the new asks.
Any use case funded before scoring because a senior sponsor asked for it directly.
Evaluation capacity below one named evaluator per three active pilots.
No stopped work to report after a full year - a portfolio where nothing ever dies is not being managed.
A smaller portfolio that finishes beats a large one that announces.
Capacity is the strategy. Fund people before platforms.
The kill list is your credibility with finance and with auditors alike.
strategy

Northbridge runs a hub-and-service model. A small central AI office owns standards, evaluation methods, the register and supplier frameworks. Service departments own their use cases, their data quality and their outcomes. Neither half works alone: central without services builds demos nobody adopts; services without central build ten incompatible tools and one shared incident.
AI policy, risk tiers and gate standards The resident outcome and the service baseline
Evaluation methods, test sets and red-team practice Case data quality and published guidance accuracy
The public AI register and transparency reporting The accountable decision-maker for every case
Supplier frameworks, model inventory and exit tests Frontline training, feedback and incident reporting
Shared platforms: retrieval, transcription, translation Channel mix, including phone, paper and in-person

The central office stays small on purpose - Northbridge caps it at fourteen staff - because its product is standards and evidence, not delivery theatre. Delivery capacity sits in the services, close to the casework.
Keep the centre small and senior. Its authority comes from standards people actually use.
Ownership follows the outcome: whoever owns the wait time owns the use case.
One register, one risk framework, one evaluation method - or none of them will be believed.
strategy

Most AI failures in government are authority failures first: nobody was clearly empowered to stop the system, so nobody did. Decision rights are written down before deployment and tested in the first incident drill.
Decision Decides Must be consulted Can stop the system
Approve a new use case Service owner, through the gates
Service owner Evaluation lead Any officer who detects resident harm, pending review
Accountability officer Service owner, communications
Renew or exit a supplier Procurement board AI office, service owner AI office, if exit or evaluation clauses are breached
The stop right matters most. A frontline officer who sees a pattern of wrong outputs can raise a harm
report that pauses the affected function pending review - without needing permission, and without career
risk. Northbridge rehearses this twice a year, the way it rehearses fire drills.
Test decision rights in drills. Untested rights are decorative.
Write the stop right into job descriptions and contracts, not just the policy PDF.
Ambiguity about authority is a decision too - it decides that the vendor's default wins.
strategy
The record as architecture: decision logs, evidence and appeal routes kept where auditors and residents can reach them.

Northbridge maintains a public AI register. Every live system has an entry a resident can read in five minutes: what it does, which service it supports, what data it uses, whether it influences a decision, who is accountable by name and role, how it is evaluated, and how to ask for a human review or appeal.

Decision logs. For any AI-influenced case, the record shows what the system suggested, what evidence it used, and what the officer decided. Logs are records, retained under the same schedule as the case file.
Incident reporting. AI incidents - wrong guidance at scale, biased outputs, data leakage - are logged, graded and summarised in a quarterly public report, including near misses.
Reasons on request. A resident affected by an AI-influenced decision can get a plain-language explanation and a human re-decision. The explanation is written for the resident, not for the regulator.
Name accountable roles publicly. Anonymous accountability is none.
Publish before you are asked. A register launched after a scandal is read as concealment.
Incident transparency compounds: each honest report makes the next one easier and cheaper.
strategy
S2 Design: the service design, data flow, human oversight point and appeal route are drawn, tested with residents, and costed end to end - before any build or buy decision.
A service blueprint showing every channel, including phone, paper and in-person, and where the human decides.
User research with residents who have low digital access, limited English, or disabilities - not only confident online users.
A data-flow map: what data, from where, under what legal basis, retained how long, visible to whom.
An oversight design: sampling rates, review queues, and the exact point where a human can override - and how overrides are recorded.
A whole-life cost (Template 4) including evaluation, translation, accessibility and exit.
The design only works for residents who complete everything online, first time, in English.
No named point of human decision in an AI-influenced case journey.
The appeal route is "contact us" with no named process, owner or timescale.
If the appeal route is not designed, the service is not designed.
Design for the hardest case first; the easy cases take care of themselves.
Cost the non-digital channels honestly. They are part of the service, not a legacy embarrassment.
strategy

Every government AI programme discovers the same truth in month three: the model is fine and the data is the problem. Addresses in four formats, case notes as scanned handwriting, guidance pages contradicted by newer circulars. Strategy means funding the boring work first.

Guidance before generation. Any system that answers residents retrieves from a single, owned, version-controlled guidance source. If two pages disagree, the fix is editorial, not technical - assign an owner to the truth.
Case data quality. Measure completeness and accuracy of the fields a use case depends on, publish the figures internally, and set a minimum bar before pilot (Gate S3).

Records by design. Prompts, outputs, model versions and officer decisions in AI-influenced cases are records. Retention, disclosure and legal-hold rules are agreed with the records team before launch, not after the first public records request arrives.
No shadow training data. Resident data is not used to train or fine-tune any model - internal or vendor - without an explicit legal basis, a register entry and an opt-out where the law requires one.
Northbridge lesson: the benefits intake pilot spent its first six weeks not on the model but on reconciling
214 guidance documents into 96 owned pages. Error rates fell before the AI switched on - a result the
programme reported honestly, and which made its later AI claims believable.
Fund data cleaning as strategy, visibly. It is where the returns start.
One owned source of guidance truth, or every channel invents its own.
Treat AI outputs as records from day one. Retrofitting retention is where programmes get hurt.
strategy
Interoperability and identity, without the mega- platform
Joined-up government does not require one giant system. It requires shared standards, lawful data sharing and a resident who only has to prove who they are and what happened once.
Identity One resident sign-in, with assisted and in-person alternatives
No one is locked out of a statutory service for failing digital identity checks
Data sharing Written agreements per purpose, logged access, tell-us-once for life events
Purpose limitation: shared for the stated service, not for general profiling
Open standards, documented interfaces, exportable data
No supplier may hold case data in a format the state cannot read without them
Case view A joined view for complex cases, assembled at point of need
Officers see what their role requires - not a universal resident dossier

The distinction in the last row matters. Interoperability serves the resident's case; a universal dossier serves the institution's curiosity. The strategy funds the first and forbids the second without explicit statutory authority.
One operations picture across permits, roadworks and service queues - shared situational awareness, not shared dossiers.
Tell-us-once is a resident right with a log attached, not a data grab.
Standards before platforms. A standard outlives every vendor in the room.
Interoperability proposals get the same public value test as AI proposals.
strategy

Government buys AI badly when it buys the demo: a polished presentation on clean data, priced per seat, with the state's data as the switching cost. Northbridge procures against the service problem, on real (anonymised) case material, with the exit rehearsed at signing.
Evaluate on our data. Shortlisted suppliers run the same held-out set of real cases. Scores are recorded and become contractual baselines.
Price the whole life. Licences, integration, data preparation, evaluation, training, translation, and exit and migration - in one number, over the contract term (Template 4).
Contract for change. Model versions, material changes and sub-processors are notified in advance; the state may re-test after any material change and suspend if performance falls below baseline.
Data terms. State data is not used to train the supplier's general models. Ever. This clause is non- negotiable and its breach ends the contract.
Exit that works. Data export in open formats, prompt and configuration escrow where relevant, and an annual exit test - an actual export, inspected, not a clause admired on paper.
An untested exit clause is a hope, and hope is not leverage.
The demo is the supplier's best day. Contract for their average day, measured on your cases.
If a supplier will not accept evaluation rights, they are telling you what their product is worth.
strategy

Every model in use - bought, built, or embedded inside another product - sits in one inventory with an owner, a version, an evaluation status and a review date. Embedded AI is the quiet risk: the case- management upgrade that quietly adds auto-summarisation, the office suite that adds drafting. Procurement and IT change processes must ask the AI question on every change, however small.
System, supplier, model and version You cannot govern what you cannot name; version changes change behaviour
Use case, service owner, risk tier Accountability attaches to a person and a tier, not to a product
Data used and legal basis The first question in any audit, complaint or legal challenge
Evaluation baseline and last test date Performance drifts; the date tells you whether anyone would know
Human oversight point and stop owner The person who can pause it, reachable in an incident
Contract end and exit test date Renewal should never arrive as a surprise with no alternative
Drift is normal; surprise is not. Re-test on every material model change and at least annually,
and treat a supplier who resists re-testing as a risk finding in themselves.
Hunt the embedded AI. It enters through upgrades, not procurements.
Version discipline is safety discipline in a world of silent model updates.
The inventory is a working tool reviewed monthly, not an annual compliance artefact.
strategy
S3 Readiness: baseline data captured, evaluation set built, staff trained, oversight staffed and a rollback rehearsed - before a single resident touches the system.
Baseline metrics locked and stored (Template 3): wait, error, completion, cost per case, and fairness breakdowns - measured before, never reconstructed after.
An evaluation set of real, anonymised cases with agreed correct outcomes, held out from any supplier tuning.
Accuracy and fairness thresholds set in advance, with the pause triggers written down (page 22).
Frontline training completed and a staffed review queue, with named cover for absence.
A rollback plan that has been executed once in rehearsal: how the service runs tomorrow if the system is switched off tonight.
No baseline - "we will measure improvement later" is a fail, in those words if necessary.
The evaluation set was built or seen by the supplier whose system it tests.
Rollback depends on the supplier's cooperation to restore the previous process.
Readiness is mostly measurement. If you cannot prove it worked, assume it did not.
Baselines locked before launch are the programme's pension - protect them.
Rehearse the rollback. The first execution should not be during the incident.
strategy
Controls scale with consequence. Northbridge tiers every use case at design and re-tiers it whenever its scope, data or decision role changes.
Staff drafting, summarisation, search; no resident impact
Guidance, translation, status answers sourced to published text
Retrieval-only answers, source citation, sampling, feedback route on every answer
Pre-set accuracy and fairness thresholds, human decision on every case, decision logs, quarterly public reporting
Triage, prioritisation, document assessment that shapes an officer's work
Anything approaching eligibility, enforcement or liberty
Presumption against deployment; executive and legal sign-off, independent evaluation, published impact assessment - and the stop list still applies

Tier creep is the characteristic failure: a T2 guidance tool slowly starts ranking cases and becomes T3 without anyone re-approving it. The inventory review (page 19) compares what the system does now against the tier it was approved at, and treats silent expansion as an incident.
Tier the behaviour, not the intention. What it does decides.
Treat tier creep as an incident, because unmanaged scope is how harm arrives quietly.
strategy

A system that is accurate on average can still be unjust in distribution - worse for one language group, one disability, one neighbourhood. Northbridge therefore tests before launch and monitors after it, by the breakdowns that matter for each service.

Test by group. Accuracy, completion and wait outcomes broken down by language, disability, age, channel and, where lawful and appropriate, ethnicity. Gaps beyond the pre-set threshold pause expansion, automatically.
Accessible by design. Plain language at a tested reading level, screen-reader and assisted channels tested with disabled residents, human help reachable without a digital dead end.
Notice. When AI influences a case, the resident is told - in the decision letter, in plain words, with the route to a human re-decision stated beside it.

Appeal that works. Appeals go to a human with the full record, a named timescale, and outcomes tracked: if appeals against AI-influenced decisions succeed at a higher rate, that is a system finding, not a resident problem.
Northbridge example: the multilingual guidance pilot improved overall completion by 11 points but only 2
points for one language group, because the translation handled formal phrasing and missed the colloquial
terms residents actually used. Expansion paused, the language data was rebuilt with community
reviewers, and the gap closed before scale. The pause was published in the quarterly report - and cited
by residents' groups as a reason to trust the programme.
Average performance hides distributional harm. Always ask: for whom is it worse?
A pause for equity, published honestly, builds more trust than a flawless launch claim.
strategy
Security, privacy and fraud: assume a motivated reader

Public services hold data residents were compelled to give. That raises the bar: the state did not earn this data in a market transaction, and residents cannot withdraw it. Security and privacy design starts from that obligation.
Data minimisation in prompts. Systems receive the fields the task needs, not the whole case file. Prompt and retrieval logs are reviewed for accidental exposure of personal data.

Prompt injection and leakage. Resident-facing retrieval is tested against attempts to extract other residents' data, internal instructions and restricted guidance. Red-team results are part of Gate S4 evidence.

Fraud, honestly balanced. AI-assisted fraud detection runs under the same due-process rules as any triage: it prioritises human investigation, it never itself determines fraud, and false-positive rates are monitored by group, because a false accusation by the state is a serious harm.
Supplier security. Data residency, sub-processor lists, breach notification within a contracted window, and the state's right to audit - verified, not attested.
Incident readiness. A named playbook for AI incidents that joins the existing security and communications plans, with pre-agreed public wording for the common cases.
Test leakage before launch; residents will test it after.
Compelled data, higher duty. Design as if every log will one day be read aloud.
Fraud savings claims must be net of false-positive harm, or they are fiction.
strategy
S4 Proof: a time-boxed pilot against the locked baseline, with pre-registered success and stop criteria, independently evaluated - and a real possibility of a no.
Pre-registered criteria (Template 5): the metrics, thresholds, fairness breakdowns and duration, filed before the pilot starts and not edited afterwards except by a logged amendment.
Independent evaluation - by the central office or an external evaluator, never by the supplier or the delivery team marking its own work.
Resident and staff feedback gathered deliberately, including from people who abandoned the service mid-journey.
Full cost accounting for the pilot, including staff time and evaluation, so scale economics are real.
A stop, fix or scale recommendation with the evidence attached, decided at a gate review the sponsor attends.
Success criteria written or revised after results were seen.
Pilot users cherry-picked from the easiest cases or the most digital residents.
A pilot with no end date. Permanent pilots are unaccountable deployments wearing a lanyard.
Protect the pilot's right to fail; a pilot that cannot fail teaches nothing.
Independent evaluation is what separates a programme from a sales channel.
Publish pilot results either way. The no results are the ones the public remembers you sharing.
strategy
Register live, baselines locked, guidance consolidated, first two Wave 1 pilots running
S0-S3 gate records complete and published in summary
Wave 1 results published, supplier framework retendered on evaluation terms, staff copilot rollout
At least two pilots pass S4 with equity breakdowns reported
Year 2 Wave 2 resident-facing assistance in three services, multilingual front door, permit completeness checks
Wave 1 services holding gains at scale; no unresolved fairness pauses
Year 3 Wave 3 tell-us-once for two life events, proactive entitlement prompts with human confirmation
Independent assurance review (Volume 10 method) with findings published

Dates are planning aids; the evidence column is the commitment. If the evidence is not there, the roadmap slips and the slip is announced with the reason - a habit that costs a headline once and buys credibility for years.
What is deliberately not on the roadmap: automated eligibility decisions, predictive enforcement
targeting, and any resident scoring. Naming the exclusions on the roadmap page itself prevents their
Publish the roadmap with its evidence conditions attached.
Announce slips with reasons. Silence converts a delay into a scandal.
Keep the exclusions printed on the roadmap, where future planners will see them.
strategy

AI in government succeeds or fails at the caseworker's desk. Staff who fear the programme will route around it, and their workarounds will be invisible to the dashboards. Northbridge treats workforce change as a first-class workstream, not a communications task.

No-surprises commitment. A published commitment on how roles change: AI absorbs transcription, search and drafting first; role changes are negotiated, trained for, and never announced by press release before they are discussed with staff and unions.
Skills, in work time. Every affected role gets role-specific training - prompting, verification, override judgement, record-keeping - delivered in working hours with backfill, not as homework.

Professional judgement protected. Guidance states plainly: the officer's judgement prevails over the system, overrides are recorded without penalty, and a pattern of overrides is treated as system feedback.

New roles, honestly counted. Evaluation, data stewardship, AI oversight and community language review are real new jobs. The strategy counts them in the economics instead of pretending the programme is costless to run.
Training in work time, with backfill - or it is a poster, not a programme.
Negotiate role change early. Surprised workforces do not adopt, they endure.
Overrides are data and professional rights at once. Protect both.
strategy
The measurement framework (Template 6) has four families, reported quarterly, in public, with the same definitions every time.
Outcomes Wait to resolution, first-contact resolution, error and rework rates, backlog age
Equity Completion, wait and accuracy gaps by language, disability, age and channel
Trust Appeal rates and success rates, complaint themes, resident survey confidence, register readership
Whether the public believes the system is on their side
Economics Cost per resolved case, whole-life cost against the business case, evaluation cost as a share of programme cost

Two disciplines keep the numbers honest. Definitions are versioned and changes are footnoted in the report where they first appear. And every favourable headline metric is published beside its equity breakdown, so good averages cannot smuggle in bad distributions.
Report the misses on the same page as the hits. A quarterly report that residents and

Every other volume in this series deals in days, weeks and budgets. This one deals in minutes - sometimes seconds. A call answered faster, a location pinned tighter, a unit sent sooner: those are the gains. The design problem is therefore sharp: take every second AI can safely give back, and give nothing of judgement away.

Structured triage protocols save lives because they ask the question a stressed human might skip. AI support makes the protocol easier to follow under pressure: the next key question surfaced, answers captured from speech, elapsed-time and red-flag prompts shown quietly. The grading decision - category, priority, response - is made by the call-taker or clinician, and the system records who graded, on what answers.
Prompts advise, they do not gate. A call-taker can always move faster than the protocol when the caller's words demand it.
Red flags escalate automatically to a human - breathing difficulty, weapons, a child alone - but nothing de-escalates automatically.
Under-triage is the audited error. Over-triage costs resources; under-triage costs people. Review samples weight the errors accordingly, and any AI change is tested for its under-triage effect first.
A caller in extremis never hears a protocol being wrestled with. The support is silent when it works.
Every grade must be explainable from the recorded answers - not from a model score.

An emergency service that only works fluently in one language, in a clear voice, on a good line, is a service for the easiest emergencies. Northbridge's call mix includes 40-plus languages in a year, text- based contact from deaf callers, silent calls that are sometimes nothing and sometimes a person who cannot speak safely.

Real-time translation, both ways, with the original audio and words preserved and shown beside the translation. Safety-critical terms - symptoms, weapons, fire locations - are rendered by approved phrase sets where they exist, and uncertainty is flagged, never smoothed over.
Text and relay parity. Text, video-relay and app contacts enter the same queue discipline and the same triage, with transcription native rather than bolted on.

Silent-call handling stays human-led. AI may detect sounds, keywords or patterns in the background audio and surface them to the call-taker. It never classifies a silent call as a hoax and never ends one.

The caller using their second language in a crisis gets the same calm and the same speed of help.

Storms, major incidents and New Year's midnight share a shape: call volume multiplies faster than staffing can. Surge is where AI helps most visibly and fails most dangerously, because every shortcut is taken exactly when scrutiny is thinnest.

Duplicate detection becomes the front line: fifty calls about one motorway collision are linked into one incident with fifty witnesses, and callers reporting the known incident are offered a fast confirmation path - staffed by humans, with the full triage one step away, never a dead end.

Non-emergency deflection is honest: callers told truthfully that this line is overwhelmed, given the alternative channel and a callback commitment - not held in a silent queue by a soothing recording.
Overflow agreements activate: partner centres take calls on shared protocols, with the same AI support and the same stop list, rehearsed twice a year, not negotiated mid-storm.

Surge capacity is bought in peacetime: overflow agreements, linked-incident tooling, rehearsed fallbacks.

Control rooms hear from the same addresses and the same voices, often for years: the resident with dementia who calls nightly, the household where calls keep ending abruptly, the caller whose "minor" reports form a pattern no single call reveals. Patterns are surfaced to people who can help: repeat-caller and repeat-address summaries go to a named human reviewer - a safeguarding lead, a neighbourhood team, a clinician - who decides whether a welfare referral, a care-plan contact or no action is right.

During a major incident, the information vacuum fills within minutes - with old footage, wrong locations and confident invention. The centre's duty is not to police the internet; it is to be the fastest reliable source in its own incident, and to correct the specific falsehoods that change behaviour or endanger crews.

Monitoring is scoped to the incident: AI tools scan public channels for the incident's places, claims and imagery, and surface rising falsehoods to the communications officer. Standing surveillance of the public is out of scope and out of policy.

Emergency recordings are evidence, disclosure material and, for the people on them, often the worst minutes of their lives. AI redaction and summarisation make disclosure feasible at volume; they also create a new way to fail a victim, by missing the one detail that should never have left the building.

Redaction is drafted by AI and verified by a person, with verification sampling rates set by the sensitivity of the material - and 100 percent verification for anything involving children, victims of sexual offences, or protected identities under law.

Summaries are labelled and linked: every AI summary carries a link to the underlying recording and transcript, and is marked as a summary wherever it travels. A summary quoted in court without its source is a process failure, owned by the process.

Retention follows the schedule, not the storage bill: recordings, transcripts, AI drafts and logs each have retention rules set by law and inquiry practice. Cheap storage is not an argument for keeping everything forever.
Access is logged at person level. Who listened, who exported, who shared - reviewable, and reviewed.
The audit trail of access is as important as the redaction itself. Sample it monthly.

Call-takers absorb trauma by ear, at volume, with seconds between calls. AI changes this exposure in both directions, and an honest programme measures both. The control room's AI will fail: a model outage, a telephony fault, a bad update, a cyber incident (the attacker's view is the AI Security Series' territory; here the duty is continuity). The question this page answers is what the room does in the first sixty seconds of that failure - because a room that has rehearsed it barely notices, and a room that has not, improvises at the worst moment.
Failure is announced, not discovered: the desk's AI status indicator (page 21) turns, an audible and logged alert fires, and the shift commander declares fallback mode on the record.

Northbridge audited 2,000 closed cases before automating anything. A third of elapsed time was waiting for evidence the county already held in another system. One in five applications was touched eleven times or more. Letters went out that applicants could not act on, generating calls, generating more letters. Touches: how many times a case is opened without progress. Every touch without a decision, a request or an update is waste with a timestamp.
Waits: where cases sit, for how long, and waiting for whom - applicant, another agency, or an internal queue nobody owns.
Rework: evidence re-requested, forms re-sent, assessments redone because the first record could not be trusted or found.
Failure demand: contacts caused by unclear letters, missed deadlines and unexplained refusals - demand the service created itself.

percent of licence applications incomplete on arrival; 18 percent of refused applications overturned on
reconsideration - the clearest sign the first decision process, not the applicants, needed fixing.

Most refused applications were never eligible; most eligible residents never apply. Both failures start in the same place: criteria written as statute, published as PDFs, and understood by neither group. Eligibility work begins before the form.

A checker that helps, not decides. An AI-guided eligibility checker asks only the questions the rules need, explains why each is asked, and ends with "likely", "unlikely" or "unclear - talk to us", never a determination. Its answers create no record used against the applicant.

Worked examples. Three anonymised examples per scheme - granted, refused, borderline - teach more than forty pages of guidance.

Most casework is not new applications; it is life continuing - a child born, a job lost, a landlord selling, a licence holder expanding. Systems designed only for intake make residents re-prove an entire life to report one change.

Time is a resource, allocated deliberately. Complex cases carry longer appointments, flexible evidence deadlines and proactive contact. The system flags approaching deadlines to the worker, never as automated warnings to the resident.
Support is recorded once, honoured everywhere. Communication needs, safe contact methods, advocates and interpreters sit on the record and shape every letter, call and appointment automatically.
AI stays in the back office here. Summaries, chronologies, drafting administration - yes. Outbound contact with a vulnerable resident is human, considered and timed, always.

outcomes and trust, or the system will rush exactly the people it most owes care.

Casework records hold safeguarding signals in plain sight: a child's absence pattern, a carer's exhaustion, coercion in a licensing visit, a sudden change in who collects a payment. AI's role is narrow and vital: notice patterns across a large record, and put them in front of a trained human the same day.
Flag, never conclude. The system raises a signal with the underlying record entries attached. It does not score a family, label a household, or write its inference into the case summary.
Same-day human review. Every signal is reviewed by a designated safeguarding professional within the working day; the review outcome - action, monitor, no concern - is recorded by that professional.

False positives are expected and costed. Thresholds are set with safeguarding leads, tuned on reviewed outcomes, and the burden of a false alarm is counted honestly; a system tuned to never be wrong will miss the case that mattered.
Access is restricted and logged. Safeguarding signals are visible only to roles with the duty and the training; every view is logged.

The tax gap - the difference between what is lawfully due and what is collected - is usually reported as one number and imagined as one cause: dishonesty. Northbridge decomposed its gap before automating anything, and found the familiar shape: most of it was error, misunderstanding, late filing and unclaimed complexity; deliberate evasion was the smallest and most expensive slice.
Failure to take reasonable care: wrong figures, missed deadlines, misunderstood reliefs - the largest, cheapest-to-fix component, fixed by design, not enforcement.
Legal interpretation: genuine disputes about what the law means, resolved by rulings and appeals, not penalties.
Non-payment: tax assessed correctly and simply not paid - a debt problem (page 17), often a hardship problem in disguise.
Evasion and fraud: deliberate concealment - the slice that justifies investigation powers, and the only slice that does.
Northbridge baseline (illustrative): an estimated gap of 6.8 percent of liabilities; 41 percent attributed to
error and failure to take care, 19 percent to non-payment, 14 percent to interpretation disputes, and 11
percent to evasion - with the remainder unregistered activity the service could barely see, let alone pursue.
Treat the decomposition as the strategy. A service that spends its AI budget hunting the 11 percent while the 41 percent files confused returns has chosen theatre over revenue.
Publish the gap by cause, not just by size; the causes point at completely different tools.
Confusion is a service defect. Count the queries a clear notice would have prevented.
An unknown slice is a measurement problem first; do not let it justify a surveillance programme by default.

Say what is proposed, plainly. A one-page, model-generated summary - height, homes, access, trees, construction - checked by the case officer before publication, with the full drawings one click away.

Reach beyond the usual voices. Site notices, neighbour letters and accessible digital routes, with response windows that respect real lives; targeted outreach where past responses skew unrepresentative.

Summarise by issue, cite by letter. Clustering groups representations by material consideration - traffic, daylight, design, drainage - each cluster cited to the letters in it, counts stated, duplicates and campaigns identified openly.

A permission is only as good as its conditions. Vague, duplicated or unmeasurable conditions convert a good decision into years of dispute - and AI is genuinely useful here, checking draft conditions against the tests every condition must pass.
The condition tests - machine-checked, planner-decided
Necessary: tied to a harm or requirement identified in the assessment, cited to it. The checker flags orphan conditions carried over from habit.
Relevant and precise: names what must be done, submitted or built, to what standard, by when - with the trigger point (before commencement, before occupation) explicit.
Enforceable and checkable: states the evidence that will discharge it and who verifies it. If no evidence could prove compliance, the condition is rewritten or dropped by the planner.
Consistent: checked against the drawings, the obligations agreement and any consultee wording for contradiction - the classic failure where two documents demand different things.

Legal agreements and planning obligations follow the same discipline: heads of terms tracked, viability evidence summarised with its assumptions visible, drafting owned by lawyers, and the completed obligations published with the decision. Community infrastructure contributions are reconciled publicly - what was promised, what was paid, what it built.
Fund condition quality as build quality; the cheapest defect is the one never conditioned badly.
Applicants get the draft condition set before decision on majors - surprises help nobody, including the authority at appeal.

Inspections, discharge and enforcement: risk-based, human-led

Permissions are promises about the future. Inspection and enforcement keep them - and this is where Volume 1's stop list bites hardest: enforcement selects where coercive power falls, so AI schedules and surfaces, and officers choose and act.

Condition discharge as a service. Submissions checked for completeness on arrival like applications (page 11), evidence compared to the condition wording, discharge signed by an officer - with a clock, because sites stall on silent desks too.

Risk-based inspection. Visit priority scored on harm potential, condition deadlines, developer history and complaints - the ranked list is a recommendation an inspector lead approves and can override, with overrides logged.

As-built comparison. Photographs, measurements and completion evidence compared to approved drawings; discrepancies triaged as trivial, regularisable or breach - by an officer, on a visit where it matters.

Enforcement with proportionality. Reports from the public acknowledged and triaged transparently; action follows the published enforcement plan - harm, intent, history - never a model's suspicion score, and never by neighbourhood targeting.
The permitting operations room: stages, clocks and queues visible to the whole team - no application waiting without an owner.
Publish inspection and enforcement service standards and performance against them.

Applicants can appeal refusals and conditions; third parties can challenge lawfulness. Each challenge is expensive for everyone - and each one is precise data about where the first decision process failed or the law genuinely sits unclear.
Classify every outcome. Dismissed, allowed on a reason the authority could have handled, allowed on a judgement call, costs awarded - the classes have different owners and different fixes.

Feed the code and the training. Allowed appeals change the rules engine tests, the guidance the model reads, the condition library and the case officer training - from one change record, like a code change (page 10).
Defend with the file, not around it. The appeal statement is assembled from the record - report, trace, summary, visit notes - which is why pages 13-18 insist the record is complete at decision time.

Costs discipline. Costs follow unreasonable behaviour; an authority that defends the indefensible pays twice. Early senior review of every appeal, with a settle-or-concede route, is cheaper and more honest.

Morning pack, not morning archaeology. Each active case opens on its parcel pack, code trace, consultation summary and next action - assembled overnight, cited, dated.
One queue, visible priorities. Cases ordered by statutory clock, harm and readiness, set by the team lead - not by whoever emailed last or loudest.
Protected judgement blocks. Site visits, negotiation and report-weighing time ring-fenced in the diary; the tools serve the blocks, they do not fragment them with alerts.
Override is normal and logged. Disagreeing with a check, a draft or a ranking is one click with a reason - and overrides are reviewed as system feedback, never as staff failure.

Failed contracts are usually described at the point they collapse: missed milestones, disputed invoices, a supplier in trouble. Northbridge reviewed its last forty troubled contracts before automating anything, and found the causes sat far earlier - in vague needs, copied specifications, unchallenged incumbent advantage and evaluations that scored the bid document, not the delivery.
Demand failure: buying the wrong thing, or the right thing twice - no owner, no demand challenge, no check against what is already contracted.

Management failure: a sound award left unmanaged - no performance data, no early warning, no relationship until the dispute letter.

Data return, verified: return in open, documented formats within the contracted window, followed by certified deletion. Sample the returned data; a transfer that cannot be loaded is a transfer that did not happen.
Transition assistance: parallel running, knowledge transfer and reasonable cooperation with the successor are contracted duties with prices agreed at award (page 17).
Continuity for residents: the exit plan names the resident-facing risks - appointments, payments, cases in flight - and the point at which no resident can tell the supplier changed.
Lessons filed: a short, honest exit review - what the competition got right, what the contract missed, what management missed - goes to the library the next specification writer will use (page 9).
Test exit like you test failure: an annual paper exercise, a sampled data return, a runbook
read by a stranger. Untested exit is a hope, not a clause.
Exit readiness is reported beside performance; a high-performing hostage is still a hostage.
Deletion certificates and returned- data samples are filed - exit evidence outlives the relationship.
Suppliers who exit well win references; make good departure part of the market's reward structure.

The procurement officer desk, workforce and the working day

Procurement judgement is a profession: commercial skill, legal literacy and market knowledge, exercised under scrutiny. AI support should return officers' time to judgement - and the workforce plan should treat that judgement as the asset it is.
The procurement desk: bids, benchmarks and the record - preparation done, judgement still to come.
The desk: one view per competition and contract - documents, timeline, bids, benchmarks, signals and the record - prepared by AI support, decided by the officer.
Skills that now matter more: specification writing, evaluation design, negotiation, data literacy and AI evidence appraisal. Bid-processing speed matters less every year.
Rotation and conflicts: officers rotate across categories on a planned cycle; declarations of interest are refreshed per competition, not per career (page 25).
Capacity honesty: competitions per officer and contracts per manager are capped by tier. Overloaded commercial staff is how stop-list lines get crossed quietly.
Officers are served by preparation that cites its sources - every summary traceable to a bid page.
Desk design is co-designed with officers; their veto on workflow changes is real.
Invest in commercial capability before procurement technology; tools amplify the judgement that exists.

Public money buys in public. Transparency in procurement is not a publication chore after award; it is the mechanism that keeps every earlier page of this volume honest.
Publish by default: opportunities, award notices, contract values, extensions and direct-award justifications appear on the public register on a fixed timetable - including the unflattering entries.

Conflicts, declared and managed: interests are declared per competition by evaluators, advisers and decision-makers; a declared conflict is managed on the record, an undeclared one discovered later is a disciplinary matter.
Gifts and hospitality: a simple rule, visibly kept: nothing from bidders during a live competition, and a register that oversight can inspect without asking twice.

Commercial confidentiality, bounded: genuinely sensitive pricing and trade secrets are protected in narrow, time-limited redactions - with the redaction itself justified. Confidentiality is a scalpel, not a curtain.
Respond to scrutiny as a service: freedom-of-information requests, audit queries and press questions about awards are answered from the record, promptly and without reconstruction (page 5).

Savings are procurement's favourite number and its least audited. Northbridge counts them the way auditors wish everyone did: baselined, whole-life, and net of the cost of buying and managing.
Baseline before competition: the current whole-life cost, independently checked, recorded in the demand note (page 9). No baseline, no saving - only a price.

Categories kept separate: cashable savings (budget actually falls), cost avoidance (a rise prevented, evidenced against an index) and value improvement (better outcomes at the same cost) are reported in separate lines, never blended into one headline.
Count the costs of buying: officer time, legal support, AI tooling, evaluation effort and bidder burden are real costs of the route chosen; efficient routes are an economic decision (page 12).
Verify at delivery: savings are re-checked at months 6 and 18 against actual spend and performance. Savings that evaporate become lessons in the specification library, with names and numbers.
Illustrative arithmetic: a competition reporting 4.2 million saved at award re-verified at 3.1 million at
month 18 - 0.6 million lost to volume growth honestly reported, 0.5 million to change requests the
specification should have covered. Publishing the second number is what makes the first one believable.
Honest savings arithmetic costs a headline and buys a decade of credibility with finance.
Suppliers price Northbridge's competence; confused buying is a cost line in every bid.
The re-verification duty sits with procurement, not with the service that enjoyed the saving.

Incident route: a suspected fairness failure pauses the competition clock, not just the tool. Legal and the awarding officer are informed the same day; bidders are told what fairness requires them to be told.
Remedy honesty: where a failure may have affected an award, Northbridge re-runs the affected stage or the competition - the cost of re-running is the price of a register people trust (page 25).
Failure drills run annually with legal, procurement and audit at the same table.
A paused competition is recoverable; a corrupted award follows the contract for its whole term.
Suppliers report suspected unfairness through a named route, answered by officers outside the competition.

1. Challenge the demand before you draft the tender.
2. Specify outcomes; never hold the competition in the specification.
3. Fix criteria and weights before bids are opened - and publish them.
4. Equal information to every bidder, at the same time, in the same words.
5. AI drafts, compares and warns; officers specify, evaluate and award.
6. Never show an evaluator an indicative score before their own.
7. One supplier's bid never informs another's - in any system, ever.
8. Test AI performance on your own cases, segmented, before award.
9. Contract for change: notice, regression evidence, rollback.
10. Contract for exit at award, while you still have leverage.
11. Price whole life - implementation, change, assurance, exit, failure.
12. Debrief every bidder like the market's memory depends on it. It does.
13. Honour standstill; a rushed signature can void a sound competition.
14. Manage contracts in tiers; fund management as a share of value.
15. Know the chain: subcontractors, sub-processors and single points of failure.
16. Pay promptly, and make primes pay promptly down the chain.
17. Publish awards, extensions and direct-award reasons on time.
18. Count savings honestly: baselined, categorised, re-verified in delivery.
19. Pause the clock, not just the tool, when fairness may have failed.
20. Renewal is a new need: every contract earns its next term at R0.
